name: reader-first-figures
reviewedBy: release steward re-anchoring the reader-first figure pass (not independent acceptance)
rationale: The reader-first figure pass of 2026-10-02 rewrote each article figure so a reader with no engineering background gets its point in five seconds: a takeaway headline, at most two visible controls with plain labels, every further control in an Adjust more fold, and the method, sources and caveats in a How this was made fold. The articles that point at those controls name them in plain words, the end-to-end specs open a fold before they use a control it now holds, and the figure sources changed with them. Each change is recorded here as exact edits over the bytes the file had before the pass. The earlier bytes stand in for the live file only while the live file is exactly the reviewed successor, so older reviews, runs and receipts that pinned them still check the bytes they recorded.

 * the same turn lowers the floor at the left and moves the hole at the right.

edits.before:
* Locomotion (quadruped stance): four near-point foot-ground contacts and a
 * stable gait attractor. The simulator's ground being off by a few
 * millimeters, or even a centimeter, is absorbed by high-bandwidth feedback;
 * the feet stay inside the tolerance band.
edits.after:
* At the left a four-legged robot stands with its hind feet on a deck, the
 * floor as the simulator modelled it, and steps its front feet down to a
 * lift plate, the real floor, which a screw jack lowers by the error. The
 * legs reach the plate, as a gait's feedback takes up the gap on its next
 * step, until the drop passes the 20 mm they can absorb; past that the front
 * feet find nothing and the robot pitches forward onto the plate.

edits.before:
* Manipulation (peg insertion): fourteen simultaneous distributed contacts
 * and a 0.5 mm clearance. The same few-millimeter contact-model error jams
 * the peg against the wall. That asymmetry, not any property of PPO, is why
 * sim-trained RL is the default for walking and not for assembly.
edits.after:
* At the right a gripper lowers a peg, the one lit part, where the simulator
 * says the hole is, and a cross-slide moves the real hole by the same error.
 * The hole leaves 0.5 mm of clearance, so the same couple of millimetres

function writeTone(group: SVGGElement | null, tone: Tone) {
  const edge = group?.querySelector('[data-live-part="edge"]');
  if (edge && edge.getAttribute('data-tone') !== tone) edge.setAttribute('data-tone', tone);
}

function writeRobotSolid(group: SVGGElement | null, solid: RobotSolid) {
  writeSolid(group, solid.paths);
  writeTone(group, solid.tone);
  const seam = group?.querySelector('[data-live-part="seam"]');
  if (seam) seam.setAttribute('d', solid.seam ?? '');
}

type Refs = {
  far: (SVGGElement | null)[];
  body: (SVGGElement | null)[];
  near: (SVGGElement | null)[];
  hatch: SVGPathElement | null;
  screws: (SVGCircleElement | null)[];
  slats: SVGPathElement | null;
  card: SVGGElement | null;
  cardFace: (SVGPathElement | null)[];
  cardEdges: SVGPathElement | null;
  pins: (SVGGElement | null)[];
  lever: (SVGGElement | null)[];
  grid: SVGPathElement | null;
  ink: SVGPathElement | null;
  pen: (SVGGElement | null)[];
};

const tenth = (value: number) => String(Math.round(value * 10) / 10);

function writeDrawing(refs: Refs, drawing: Drawing) {
  drawing.far.forEach((solid, index) => writeRobotSolid(refs.far[index] ?? null, solid));
  drawing.body.forEach((solid, index) => writeRobotSolid(refs.body[index] ?? null, solid));
  drawing.near.forEach((solid, index) => writeRobotSolid(refs.near[index] ?? null, solid));
  refs.hatch?.setAttribute('d', drawing.hatch.outline);
  refs.screws.forEach((circle, index) => {
    const point: Flat | undefined = drawing.hatch.screws[index];
    circle?.setAttribute('cx', point ? tenth(point[0]) : '0');
    circle?.setAttribute('cy', point ? tenth(point[1]) : '0');
    circle?.setAttribute('r', point ? '0.4' : '0');
  });
  refs.slats?.setAttribute('d', drawing.slats);
  refs.card?.setAttribute('transform', drawing.cardShift);
  refs.cardFace.forEach((path) => path?.setAttribute('d', drawing.card.face));
  refs.cardEdges?.setAttribute('d', drawing.card.edges);
  drawing.pins.forEach((paths, index) => writeSolid(refs.pins[index] ?? null, paths));
  drawing.lever.forEach((paths, index) => writeSolid(refs.lever[index] ?? null, paths));
  refs.grid?.setAttribute('d', drawing.grid);
  refs.ink?.setAttribute('d', drawing.ink);
  drawing.pen.forEach((paths, index) => writeSolid(refs.pen[index] ?? null, paths));
}

* ImpedanceContactLab: a one-dimensional compliant-contact lab. A
 * commanded penetration depth into a rigid surface (the position error a
 * real controller holds when the surface is 2 mm nearer than the model
 * said), a desired stiffness K and damping D, and a hardware selector with
 * three options: position-controlled geared arm, torque-controlled arm,
 * series-elastic joint.
edits.after:
* ImpedanceContactLab: a one-dimensional compliant-contact lab, drawn as a
 * press test stand (components/iso/figures/press-test-stand.ts). A head
 * slides down a column and presses a fingertip onto a glass vial on a load
 * cell; a force gauge wired to the load cell shows the push, its lit needle
 * the push now and a drag pointer the first bump, the hardest push, against
 * a shaded arc where the glass cracks. "Which arm?" swaps the head: a stiff
 * geared drive that only follows a position (it has no softness knob), an
 * arm that controls its own push (a knob on its motor sets the commanded
 * stiffness K) or the same arm with a coil spring built in. "Softness" turns
 * the knob. Press depth, damping D, the exact readouts and Reset sit in
 * "Adjust more".
 *
 * The teaching move: the stiff arm greys out softness and damping
 * with the NATIVE disabled attribute (a disabled control is honestly
 * unavailable rather than focusable-and-inert) and its push runs off the
 * gauge, because a position loop has no force channel at all.

The robot plans by imagining its future one step at a time, and each imagined step starts from the last imagined one, not from the real state. On the bench each imagined step is one section of track, bolted to the end of the section before it, and the curved steel template with a station post every five steps is the real route. A small error at one joint is carried into every later section and grows. The bench lays as many sections as the first slider says; the knob on the controller turns with the second.

The drift is a toy recurrence, not a measured model: each step adds the one-step error, scaled up by how far the imagined state has already drifted, d(t) = d(t − 1) + e × (1 + 0.02 × d(t − 1)). At {epsilonPercent.toFixed(1)}% error per step and {stepsWord(horizon)} it reaches{' '} {formatUnits(deviationNow)} units of toy latent deviation. The bench draws each unit as the same inward step off the template, read on the radius arm, and stops the track at the hub’s flange; the number keeps growing.

Dreamer learns with a decoder that turns imagined states back into pictures, drawn here as picture cards on flags along the track. TD-MPC2 has no decoder: it never draws a picture, and its drift shows up as error in the reward it predicts (“Adjust more” switches between the two). TD-MPC and TD-MPC2 are also trained to keep imagined and encoded states consistent, so a single toy number is not a complete account of either training loss.

const LINE_STEP_EM = 1.25;

/** Arrowhead of an annotation pointer, in stage units. */
export const ANNOTATION_ARROW = { length: 9, halfWidth: 4.5, gap: 3 } as const;

/**
 * The leader of an arrow pointer: it stops `gap` short of the target so the
 * head never covers the mark it names, and the head's base sits `length`
 * back along the leader. Returns null when the leader is too short to carry
 * a head.
 */
export function annotationArrow(
  from: ChartPoint,
  target: ChartPoint,
): { end: ChartPoint; head: readonly [ChartPoint, ChartPoint, ChartPoint] } | null {
  const dx = target[0] - from[0];
  const dy = target[1] - from[1];
  const length = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
  const { length: headLength, halfWidth, gap } = ANNOTATION_ARROW;
  if (length <= headLength + gap) return null;
  const ux = dx / length;
  const uy = dy / length;
  const tip: ChartPoint = [target[0] - ux * gap, target[1] - uy * gap];
  const baseX = tip[0] - ux * headLength;
  const baseY = tip[1] - uy * headLength;
  return {
    end: [baseX, baseY],
    head: [tip, [baseX - uy * halfWidth, baseY + ux * halfWidth], [baseX + uy * halfWidth, baseY - ux * halfWidth]],
  };
}

edits.before: The calculator in the reasoning panel above computes p^n at any setting. The per-step slider spans the full range on purpose, so the boundary cases are honest: at 0% per-step the task never completes once the horizon is at least one step, at 100% it always completes, and at a horizon of exactly one step the readout equals the per-step value. No setting produces a meaningless number, and the decay curve is the point. Within the same illustrative model, solving p^n = q gives p = q^(1/n). For the chosen episode target q = 0.8, n = 5 gives 95.6% and n = 30 gives 99.3%, rounded to one decimal place. These model-dependent derivations do not infer per-step reliability from real benchmark results.

edits.before: ## The economics you can drag Drag a slider such as jam-clearing time or per-pick success and the payback readout updates. Use the sliders to compare two cases in this authored model. Keep robot cost at 80,000 USD, integration at 2.5 times, cycle time at 6 seconds, uptime at 95 percent and hourly wage at 25 USD. With 15-second jam clearing, lowering per-pick success from 99.9 to 99 percent changes calculated payback from 11.56 to 11.82 months: an increase of 0.26 months, or 2.2 percent. Repeat the comparison with jam clearing set to 300 seconds: calculated payback rises from 12.11 to 17.30 months, and modeled output falls from 542.9 to 380.0 picks per elapsed hour, a 30 percent decrease. Both paybacks remain within the model's chosen 24-month horizon. These calculated results depend on assumed inputs; no deployment was measured for the comparison. The payback readout rounds to one decimal place. This calculator is an authored worked example with no measured deployment or financial forecast behind it. Its 80,000 USD robot cost is an assumed input, with no sourced arm-price quote; the 20,000 to 250,000 USD range and 5,000 USD step are chosen controls. All seven defaults, ranges and steps are authored assumptions: a 2.5 integration multiple, 6-second cycle, 95 percent uptime, 99.9 percent per-pick success, 15-second jam clearing and 25 USD hourly wage accompany that robot cost. The model also chooses 730 hours per month, a 60-month amortization period and a chosen 24-month verdict horizon. Throughput is modeled picks per elapsed hour, including downtime. Payback divides cell capital by modeled monthly labour value; it does not add damage or throughput savings. EVST supplies vendor context; the calculator's exact inputs are authored. Its guide describes complete-cell budgets, explicitly does not publish fixed list prices, and places the robot at a third to half of total cost . Its payback guidance is 12 to 24 months for multi-shift cells, extending toward 24 to 36 months for single-shift or lower-throughput operations . The calculator's 2.5 multiple and 24-month threshold are selections within that context, without quoted measurements behind them. ## What is actually automated at scale

edits.before: A manipulation task is a chain of decisions, and the chain succeeds only when every link does. If each step succeeds independently with probability $p$, an $N$-step task completes with probability $p^N$. The exponent is the whole story. A policy with 95% per-step success completes a 30-step task 21% of the time. At 99% per-step the same task completes 74% of the time. Even at 99.9% per-step, a figure almost no system publishes, a 30-step task completes 97% of the time and still fails once in thirty runs. The per-step number and the task number are different metrics, and a result reported without its horizon cannot be compared against either. Drag the per-step success slider from 95% up toward 100 and watch how late the episode number recovers, then press the presets to compare the three per-step bars over the same horizon.

edits.before: Play the scene below and step through its beats. Sixty action samples start clustered on two demonstrated strategies, jitter into one shared Gaussian cloud, and are transported back onto the two modes over the paper's 10-step DDIM inference schedule, conditioned on the observed state. edits.before: 'Running thousands of physics simulator instances at once on a single GPU so a reinforcement learning agent collects experience at a rate no CPU cluster matches. Isaac Gym made the setup practical by keeping both physics and policy training on the GPU and passing data straight from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors, skipping the CPU round-trip entirely, which bought two to three orders of magnitude in throughput over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU learner. Rudin and colleagues showed what that buys: four thousand parallel ANYmal instances trained with PPO learned flat-terrain walking in under four minutes and uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU.',
edits.after: 'Running thousands of physics simulator instances at once on a single GPU, so one workstation collects reinforcement learning experience at rates that once needed CPU clusters. Isaac Gym made the setup practical by keeping both physics and policy training on the GPU and passing data straight from physics buffers to PyTorch tensors, skipping the CPU round-trip entirely, which bought two to three orders of magnitude in throughput over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU learner. Rudin and colleagues showed what that buys: four thousand parallel ANYmal instances trained with PPO learned flat-terrain walking in under four minutes and uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU.',

edits.before: 'Control by constant re-planning: at each control step, optimize a short sequence of future actions against an explicit dynamics model, execute only the first action, and solve again from the freshly measured state. Because the plan is recomputed online, model error is rejected by feedback at every step instead of being frozen into a policy\'s weights, so a model-predictive controller shows less of the frozen-policy sim-to-real failure mode, though a wrong dynamics model still costs it closed-loop performance. Long assumed too slow for a robot\'s full dynamics, the method reached whole-body scale in 2026, when Zhang and colleagues solved iLQR against MuJoCo\'s physics fast enough to close the loop in real time on real hardware.',
edits.after: 'Control by constant re-planning: at each control step, optimize a short sequence of future actions against an explicit dynamics model, execute only the first action, and solve again from the freshly measured state. Because the plan is recomputed online, model error is rejected by feedback at every step instead of being frozen into a policy\'s weights, so a model-predictive controller shows less of the frozen-policy sim-to-real failure mode, though a wrong dynamics model still costs it closed-loop performance. Long assumed too slow for a robot\'s full dynamics, whole-body MPC now runs in real time on legged hardware: Zhang and colleagues\' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller, first posted in 2025 and revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026, closes the loop on quadruped and humanoid robots.',

### Owner decision, 10 October 2026: the research-page standard

Josef replaced the brand-v2 visual identity on every page and every figure with the research-page standard in `PANTHEON-SPEC.md`: paper and ink, hairline 1 px rules, grayscale chart tones and one muted blue accent; DM Sans 400 for the display H1 and DM Sans 600 for section heads and the wordmark; Geist 16/1.62 for body and interface text; Geist Mono for numerals, code and readouts; a single top bar, a sticky contents rail, margin sidenotes, numbered findings and booktabs tables. Wherever a brand-v2 section below disagrees, this decision governs.

- The executable palette in section 5, its renderer mirror in `lib/brand-v2-tokens.ts` and the colour rows of `contract/design-integrity.md` carry the new values.
- Web pages load DM Sans, Geist and Geist Mono through `next/font/google`, self-hosted under `/_next/static/media/`. The Tektur binaries stay checked in for the offline Open Graph renderer only: no stylesheet declares Tektur and no runtime route requests either binary. The Tektur sections below describe that renderer. The type-role registry (`data/type-roles.json`) keeps its role ids and instances; each display instance now computes DM Sans at its registered weight with no variation-axis override, and the interface and reading roles share Geist. The type rows of `contract/design-integrity.md` carry these values.
- Surfaces are plain paper. The concrete micro-texture and the halftone dot field are retired from the material registry, and `material:paper` is the one material the site paints. The texture rules in section 9 no longer have a web surface to apply to. Each named representative surface (the home masthead, the article title sheet, the domain hub header, the A-Z and glossary headers, the search sheet, and the market-map and playground headers) declares that material through `materialAttributes()` in `lib/brand-v2-materials.ts`, whose contrast verdict is computed from the ink and paper tokens; no declaration sits on or inside the prose column.
- Corners are square: every radius token is 0px and the code block's `--code-radius` (7px) is the one exception. No surface casts a shadow at any level; the radius ladder of section 8.1 and the raised and floating shadows of section 8.3 describe brand-v2 and are not used. The `/how-robots-work/` explainers keep their approved geometry (Josef, 12 October 2026).
- Every rail and rule is a 1 px `--line` hairline; a current or active-interval rail is a 1 px ink rule, never an accent bar. Registered devices carry their registry purpose and owner on the element, and the site footer's top rule is the shared registered rail on every route.
- Nothing outside an action, a compact control, media or a data figure paints a dark ground, and the site has no dark theme. Uppercase eyebrows and section heads keep `Robot Wiki`, Greek letters and units after a number in their written case (`lib/notation-case.ts`).
- Public identity, descriptor, technical identifiers, routes, citations, data truth and accessibility obligations are unchanged.
